blockers.message: the review record has no `## code.review` section, while roles were active at it
R-security-1 (API tokens are stored in clear in the database) is high and still open; fix it, or a human accepts the risk or defers it
R-security-2 (The Authorization header, and so every bearer token, is written to the logs) is high and still open; fix it, or a human accepts the risk or defers it

findings.evidence:
The `api_tokens` table holds `user_id`, `token` and `created_at`; the
middleware looks a request's token up with `WHERE token = $1`. Storing the
token as given keeps the lookup a simple indexed equality.
findings.location: design.md#Decision: Tokens are stored as given
findings.recommendation: Store only a hash of the token (SHA-256 of the 32 random bytes is enough for high-entropy tokens; no bcrypt needed) in a `token_hash` column, hash the presented bearer token in the middleware and look it up with `WHERE token_hash = $1` — still a single indexed equality, so the stated reason for storing it as given does not hold. Anyone who reads the `api_tokens` table (a database backup, a replica, a read-only SQL access, an injection elsewhere) otherwise obtains every live token and can call the API as every user who created one; with revocation deferred, those tokens stay valid indefinitely (CWE-312, CWE-256). Update tasks 1.1 and 1.2 accordingly.
findings.title: API tokens are stored in clear in the database

findings.evidence:
To diagnose integration problems, the middleware logs each request's
method, path and headers at `info` level, including `Authorization`, so
support can see which token an integration sent.
findings.location: design.md#Decision: Every request is logged with its headers
findings.recommendation: Redact the `Authorization` header (and `Cookie`) before logging; if support needs to identify the token, log the token's id or a short fingerprint of its hash, never the token itself. As designed, every request with `Authorization: Bearer <token>` puts a working credential in the logs at `info`, so anyone with access to the logs or the log pipeline (support staff, log aggregator, shipped log files) can replay it and act as the token's owner, with no way to revoke it (CWE-532). Adjust task 1.3 so `logs_requests` asserts the header is redacted.
findings.title: The Authorization header, and so every bearer token, is written to the logs

findings.recommendation: Ship at least a minimal way to invalidate a token in this change — a delete of the user's token row, or an expiry date checked by the middleware — or state the risk explicitly and get a human to accept it. The proposal's own motivation is that "a leaked integration exposes the account"; today the user can change the password to cut a leaked integration off, but with this design a token leaked from an integration's configuration keeps full API access to the account for ever, and the Risks section only answers a lost token, not a leaked one.
findings.title: A leaked token cannot be invalidated: revocation is deferred and tokens never expire
